new_statements.quote: Each word has a stressed syllable, and a compound word may have two stressed syllables. The main prosodic stress usually falls on the first syllable of the root (Bartholomew 1983: 339). Verb prefixes are not stressed, however. If the verb root begins with a vowel, the aspect marker (prefix) combines with the verb root and the primary stress is then on the first syllable which combines the prefix and root material. [p. 14] [...] I underline the stressed syllable in all examples in this dissertation to illustrate its placement but do not make the claim that stress placement is predictable. As shown by Nellis and Nellis (1983) some roots have stress elsewhere. [p. 15]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for 'Macuiltianguis Zapotec / MacZ' has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to contradict. Tejada supplies a rule: main stress on the first syllable of the root (prefixes unstressed, one stress per root in compounds), with lexical exceptions of non-initial root stress. The statement is made for SJZ = Atepec Zapotec (Bartholomew 1983 grammar) and is applied without comment to MacZ in section 3.6, where the 'stressed syllable of the verb root' is root-initial in every MacZ form cited.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word has one stressed syllable; main stress usually falls on the first syllable of the root, and verb prefixes (aspect markers) are unstressed. When a consonant-only aspect marker fuses with a vowel-initial root, stress falls on that merged first syllable. Compounds carry one main stress per root (first syllable of each root), e.g. [etta ʃtílá] 'bread', [tsuʔú latsiʔ] 'to like' (p. 14, after Bartholomew 1983: 339). All verb roots Tejada recorded had root-initial stress, cued by slight lengthening of the stressed syllable; but she declines to claim stress is predictable because the Nellis and Nellis (1983) dictionary lists roots with non-initial stress. In the MacZ section (3.6, pp. 265-269, data from Broadwell 2000) the floating 1sg H tone likewise lands on 'the stressed syllable of the verb root', which in every cited form is the root-initial syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Compounds are said to have as many main stresses as roots (two stressed syllables), not a primary/secondary distinction. Stressed syllables are slightly longer than unstressed ones (p. 15, citing Marks 1976: 117).
new_statements.exceptions: Some roots have non-initial stress according to the Nellis and Nellis (1983) dictionary; the author therefore does not claim stress placement is predictable (p. 15). Three syllable types CV, CVʔ, CVʔV; whether fortis consonants are moraic geminates is left open (p. 14 fn. 3).
new_statements.identity_note: Tejada states (pp. 5-7) that although she writes 'SJZ', all her data come from a speaker of Atepec Zapotec (San Juan Atepec, Ixtlán district, Oaxaca); she follows Foreman (2006) in treating Atepec Zapotec and Macuiltianguis Zapotec (MacZ, town of San Pablo Macuiltianguis) as dialects of one language, both often called Sierra Juárez Zapotec. The stress statement (pp. 14-15) is for Atepec Zapotec, drawn from Bartholomew's (1983) grammar in the Nellis and Nellis dictionary; section 3.6 (pp. 251-271) treats MacZ from Broadwell (2000) data and assumes the same root-initial 'stressed syllable'. The catalog item is named 'Macuiltianguis Zapotec / MacZ' under glottocode sier1250 (Sierra de Juárez Zapotec [zaa]), which per this source covers both Atepec and MacZ.

tone_statements.quote: The Otomanguean language Macuiltianguis Zapotec (=MacZ, Broadwell & Zhang 1999; Broadwell 2000; Broadwell et al. 2011; Foreman 2006; Tejada 2012)13 has three level tones and downstepped high tones (= a!1).14 The only existing tone sequences on vowels are 31 and 13 and can only surface on long vowels. This distribution follows straightforwardly from assuming that the TBU in MacZ is the μ and no true contour tones are possible in the language. … I notate the tones with the numbers high1, mid2, and low3; contra to the notation in the sources.

sources.quote: No stress rule is stated; stress is treated as a lexical property marked per word in transcription ('capitalized tone levels indicate the stressed syllable'; IPA ˈ on e.g. ˈjè.là 'night', ˈʂú.dí 'father' vs unmarked-initial gú.sàʔ 'mud'), and distributional statements presuppose both stressed and unstressed root syllables: 'Modal and checked vowels can appear in both stressed and unstressed syllables, while VʔV ... would be restricted to stressed syllables in root-final position, as in belaʔa'. Also: 'MacZ, however, retains post-tonic vowels and allows plenty of disyllabic roots'. Cites Forema
